## Methane (CH₄) — Bond Structure and Properties

### Molecular Structure

Methane (CH₄) is the simplest hydrocarbon. It consists of **one central carbon atom** covalently bonded to **four hydrogen atoms**.

---

### Type of Bond: Covalent Bonds

The bonds in methane are **single covalent bonds (C–H bonds)**. In each bond:
- The **carbon atom** shares one of its four valence electrons with one **hydrogen atom**.
- The **hydrogen atom** shares its one valence electron with carbon.
- This creates **4 shared electron pairs** (4 bonding pairs).

---

### Hybridization: sp³

The carbon atom in methane undergoes **sp³ hybridization**:
- Carbon's one **2s** orbital and three **2p** orbitals mix to form **four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals**.
- Each sp³ orbital overlaps with the **1s orbital of a hydrogen atom** to form a **sigma (σ) bond**.

---

### Geometry: Tetrahedral

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Molecular Geometry | Tetrahedral |
| Bond Angle | **109.5°** |
| Bond Length (C–H) | **109 pm (1.09 Å)** |
| Bond Energy (C–H) | **~413 kJ/mol** |
| Number of bonds | 4 (all single/sigma bonds) |

The four hydrogen atoms are arranged symmetrically around the carbon, pointing toward the **corners of a tetrahedron**, minimizing electron pair repulsion (VSEPR theory).

---

### Polarity

- Each **C–H bond** is slightly polar because carbon (electronegativity ≈ 2.5) is slightly more electronegative than hydrogen (electronegativity ≈ 2.1).
- However, due to the **symmetric tetrahedral geometry**, the bond dipoles **cancel out**, making **methane a nonpolar molecule** overall (net dipole moment = 0).

---

### Summary

> Methane has **4 equivalent sp³ C–H sigma bonds**, arranged in a **tetrahedral geometry** with bond angles of **109.5°**. It is a **nonpolar** molecule despite having slightly polar bonds.
